Introduction Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD), including neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) and detrusor sphincter dyssynergia, is one of the most frequent and devastating sequelae of spinal cord injury (SCI), as it can lead to urinary incontinence and secondary damage such as renal failure. Transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (TTNS) is a promising, non-invasive neuromodulatory intervention that may prevent the emergence of the C-fibre evoked bladder reflexes that are thought to cause NDO. This paper presents the protocol for TTNS in acute SCI (TASCI), which will evaluate the efficacy of TTNS in preventing NDO. Furthermore, TASCI will provide insight into the mechanisms underlying TTNS, and the course of NLUTD development after SCI. Methods and analysis TASCI is a nationwide, randomised, sham-controlled, double-blind clinical trial, conducted at all four SCI centres in Switzerland. The longitudinal design includes a baseline assessment period 5–39 days after acute SCI and follow-up assessments occurring 3, 6 and 12 months after SCI. A planned 114 participants will be randomised into verum or sham TTNS groups (1:1 ratio), stratified on study centre and lower extremity motor score. TTNS is performed for 30 min/day, 5 days/week, for 6–9 weeks starting within 40 days after SCI. The primary outcome is the occurrence of NDO jeopardising the upper urinary tract at 1 year after SCI, assessed by urodynamic investigation. Secondary outcome measures assess bladder and bowel function and symptoms, sexual function, neurological structure and function, functional independence, quality of life, as well as changes in biomarkers in the urine, blood, stool and bladder tissue. Safety of TTNS is the tertiary outcome. Ethics and dissemination TASCI is approved by the Swiss Ethics Committee for Northwest/Central Switzerland, the Swiss Ethics Committee Vaud and the Swiss Ethics Committee Zürich (#2019-00074). Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications. Transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (TTNS) is a well-tolerated, low-risk, non-invasive intervention. The inpatient setting facilitates study procedures and monitoring that maximise intervention adherence. Secondary outcomes provide valuable information regarding the impact of TTNS on additional factors that are relevant to patients as well as clinicians, and also facilitate targeted analyses aimed at better understanding the mechanism underlying TTNS therapy, and the development of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction after SCI. In comparison to beginning immediately after SCI, the intervention start at 29–40 days after SCI (in order to complete all baseline assessments) may modestly reduce the potential for neuroplasticity and the maximum achievable intervention effect.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Transcutaneous Tibial Nerve Stimulation (TTNS) in acute spinal cord injury (SCI) patients for preventing neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD).
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers neuroplastic changes in C-fibre-mediated spinal reflex pathways, leading to aberrant micturition reflexes and neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO). Transcutaneous Tibial Nerve Stimulation (TTNS) is a neuromodulatory intervention hypothesized to impede or alter this neuroplasticity, preventing the sensitisation of 'silent' C fibres and the formation of spinal reflex pathways responsible for NDO. The study aims to provide insight into the mechanisms underlying TTNS and the pathogenesis of NLUTD after SCI by evaluating differential changes in brain and spinal cord function, corticospinal integrity, and various biomarkers. The mechanism of neuromodulatory therapy (TTNS) is currently considered a 'black box'.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The TTNS intervention involves electrical stimulation at 20 Hz frequency, 200 µs pulse width, and a submotor current amplitude (0.5-1.0 mA below motor threshold). It is applied for 30 min/day, 5 days/week, for 6–9 weeks, starting within 40 days (specifically 29-40 days) after acute SCI. This active treatment (verum group) is compared against a sham TTNS group in a 1:1 ratio, stratified on study centre and lower extremity motor score. The sham set-up is identical in appearance and procedure but uses a 1000 Ohm resistance to prevent electrical stimulation, maintaining blinding. The study targets a detectable difference of 0.25 in the proportion of participants developing NDO between groups.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The intervention specifically targets the prevention of neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) and other neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD) by altering C-fibre sensitisation and spinal reflex pathways in patients with acute spinal cord injury (SCI). The nationwide, randomised, sham-controlled, double-blind design ensures specificity in evaluating the TTNS effect and minimizes bias. While a pilot study also reported improved erectile and bowel function, its primary focus in this context is lower urinary tract dysfunction.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients with acute spinal cord injury (SCI) admitted to rehabilitation in Switzerland, screened between 5–39 days after SCI diagnosis. Participants are stratified based on their Lower Extremity Motor Score (LEMS) at baseline (<12, 12–37, >37), which provides prognostic utility for urinary continence and complete bladder emptying at 1 year after SCI.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Prevention of neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) and other neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD), which are frequent and devastating sequelae of SCI, leading to urinary incontinence, secondary damage (e.g., renal failure, upper urinary tract damage), recurrent urinary tract infections, high intravesical pressure, and vesicoureterorenal reflux. The intervention aims to improve bladder and bowel function, sexual function, neurological function, functional independence, and quality of life (QoL) after SCI, thereby eliminating lifelong issues, lowering barriers to workforce participation, and reducing lifetime healthcare costs.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Protective benefit and preventative measure against NDO and its associated complications. The Lower Extremity Motor Score (LEMS) measured within 40 days of SCI is a reliable prognostic indicator for urinary continence and complete bladder emptying 1 year after SCI, thus providing prognostic utility for this patient population.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study is a nationwide, randomised, sham-controlled, double-blind clinical trial, indicating a robust design for evaluating the efficacy of TTNS in preventing NDO. The primary outcome, NDO occurrence, is assessed by urodynamic investigation, a standard method. The Lower Extremity Motor Score (LEMS) measured within 40 days of SCI is described as a reliable prognostic indicator for urinary continence and complete bladder emptying 1 year after SCI. While the TTNS intervention itself was found feasible and safe in a pilot study with no known safety risks, the provided text does not contain an explicit reliability assessment for NDO or other specific biomarkers themselves, beyond stating their evaluation for differential changes to understand mechanisms.
